title: Forced Authentication
summary: Forced authentication turns a victim machine into the client of an attacker controlled service, so that the machine volunteers its own credentials instead of the attacker having to guess them. The mechanism depends on a design choice in Windows networking: when a system is asked to open a network resource, it authenticates automatically as the current user rather than waiting for a prompt. Two protocols carry the resulting exchange. The Server Message Block protocol handles file sharing, and the Web Distributed Authoring and Versioning protocol, an extension of the Hypertext Transfer Protocol, acts as the fallback when SMB is blocked or fails. The delivery can be an email whose embedded resource link points to an external host, a document containing a template or image reference to a remote address, a shortcut or screen saver configuration file placed in a folder a user browses, or a file on a shared location. Whichever route is used, the machine resolves the address, connects out and completes an authentication handshake against the attacker listener, sending the challenge and response material that a hash cracking tool can attack offline for as long as the attacker likes. What the attacker obtains is a credential hash, not a password, which is why the defender's mental model matters: the connection attempt leaves the network and the material leaves in a form that supports slow offline guessing. Detection therefore leans on outbound authentication to untrusted addresses, on network protocols like SMB or WebDAV reaching the internet, on unusual file types such as shortcut or configuration files appearing in download or desktop folders, and on process telemetry showing a user application or the operating system resolving and contacting a host it has never contacted before.

beginner.definition: Computers on a network can prove who they are automatically, without asking you for a password. Forced authentication is when an attacker tricks your computer into proving its identity to a server the attacker controls.
beginner.whyItMatters: Windows sends a coded version of your password, called a password hash, without asking you. The attacker captures that code and can guess passwords against it later, offline, for as long as needed. You only have to open a document or view a folder. No warning appears and nothing seems broken.
howItWorks: Windows tries to prove your identity automatically when it reaches a network share.
The Server Message Block protocol carries file sharing, and WebDAV is its backup.
An attacker places a link, shortcut or document that points to their own server.
You open the item, or simply browse a folder that contains it.
Your computer connects out and authenticates to the machine the attacker controls.
The attacker saves the response material and cracks it offline at leisure.
beginner.example: Imagine a parcel office where the clerk must show a stamped receipt to collect a package. Someone pins a fake note to the counter saying collect here instead. The clerk walks to the fake window and stamps the receipt for a stranger. The stranger keeps the stamp print and studies it at home.
takeaways: Simply viewing a file should never send an authentication attempt off the network.
The material stolen is a hash, which an attacker cracks offline over time.
Long, random passwords are the real defence, because guessing takes too long.

objectives: Explain why Windows authenticates automatically when it reaches a network resource.
Describe how SMB and WebDAV are used to capture credential material.
Describe how a file, link or template can trigger an authentication attempt.
Identify outbound network and file artefacts that reveal forced authentication.
Explain how password length changes the attacker outcome after a hash is captured.
